claude-code.name: Claude Code
claude-code.version: Claude Code 2.1.296 (closed source: docs, changelog and --help only)

config_scopes.precedence_summary: Highest first: managed > command line (--settings) > project local (.claude/settings.local.json) > shared project (.claude/settings.json) > user (~/.claude/settings.json). Scalar keys take the highest level that sets them; list keys such as permissions.allow/deny/ask, hooks and sandbox path lists merge across levels. A deny rule at any level beats an allow at any level. Environment variables are not a level; precedence is decided per variable/key pair. A few security keys honor a stricter value from a lower level (e.g. permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories true from any scope).

paths: Server-managed: claude.ai admin console or a self-hosted Claude apps gateway; fetched at startup, polled hourly, cached locally
MDM/OS policy: macOS managed preferences domain com.anthropic.claudecode; Windows HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode value `Settings` (JSON)

File: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json (macOS); /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (Linux, WSL); C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json (Windows); plus optional managed-settings.d/*.json drop-ins merged alphabetically
managed-mcp.json in the same system directories (exclusive MCP server set)
Windows HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode `Settings` (user-writable fallback, used only when no admin source is present)
Parent settings from an embedding host via the SDK `managedSettings` option (ignored when an admin source is present unless parentSettingsBehavior is "merge")
policyHelper executable named by MDM/file source that computes managed settings at startup

scopes.notes: Server-managed settings are not fetched when a third-party provider or non-default ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is used, or when the user signs in to a different organization.

paths: Environment variables (e.g. CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB, CLAUDE_CODE_RESTRICTED), decided per pair, not as a level
Session-scoped rules saved from prompts (in memory)
.claude/settings.local.json (read and written at the git repository root since v2.1.211; in a worktree, the main checkout root)
scopes.notes: Treated as personal (allow rules apply without trust) only while git reports it untracked; if tracked or if .claude is a symlink it is treated as repository-supplied and waits for workspace trust (since v2.1.207).

paths: .claude/settings.json in the session's primary working directory (no parent-directory fallback)

allow_commands.how: permissions.allow with Bash(...) rules, or --allowedTools for one session. Granularity: exact match (no `*`), prefix (`cmd *` or legacy `cmd:*`), and glob-style `*` anywhere (matches any text including spaces). No regex. Example: {"permissions": {"allow": ["Bash(npm run test *)", "Bash(git diff *)"]}}
allow_commands.limits: Compound commands are split on &&, ||, ;, |, |&, & and newlines and every subcommand must match. A fixed set of wrappers (timeout, time, nice, nohup, stdbuf, command, builtin, noglob, bare xargs) is stripped before matching. Prefix rules cannot auto-approve exec wrappers (watch, setsid, flock, ionice) or find with -exec/-delete. Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions; on entering auto mode broad rules (Bash(*), interpreter wildcards like Bash(python*), package-manager run commands) are dropped. Allow rules never approve writes to protected paths or rm/rmdir of critical paths. Managed allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly discards all non-managed allow rules.

evidence.quote: A `*` in a Bash rule matches any text, including spaces
A rule with no `*` matches one exact command.
A rule must match each subcommand independently.
On entering auto mode, broad allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution are dropped

deny_commands.how: permissions.deny with Bash(...) rules, or --disallowedTools for one session. Example: {"permissions": {"deny": ["Bash(git push *)", "Bash(curl *)"]}}. A bare `Bash` deny removes the tool entirely.
deny_commands.limits: Hard block: deny rules apply in every mode including bypassPermissions, are evaluated before ask and allow, and a deny at any scope cannot be overridden by an allow at any other scope; the user is not offered a runtime approval for a denied call (they would have to edit settings, which they cannot do for managed rules). Deny rules match after env-assignment stripping and inside subshells, $(...) and control-flow bodies. But matching is on the command text: `/usr/bin/curl`, `sh -c 'curl ...'`, `git -C . push` are not matched. The docs state a deny rule is not a security boundary; pair with the sandbox. Exception: on machines without managed settings and not on a Team/Enterprise plan, an installed mod handling tool.check can approve a call a deny rule refuses.

evidence.quote: Deny rules block in every mode, including `bypassPermissions`.
If a tool is denied at any level, no other level can allow it.
a deny or ask rule covers the invocation Claude usually produces and isn't a security boundary around the program.
Anywhere else, the mod can approve a call that a deny rule refuses.

ask_commands.how: permissions.ask with Bash(...) rules. Example: {"permissions": {"ask": ["Bash(git push *)", "Bash(dangerouslyDisableSandbox:true)"]}}
ask_commands.limits: Ask rules prompt even in acceptEdits, auto and bypassPermissions modes, and an ask beats a more specific allow. In dontAsk mode and in -p runs with no permission host the call is denied instead of prompted. Content-scoped ask rules still prompt for sandboxed commands, but a bare `Bash` ask rule is skipped for commands that run sandboxed under autoAllowBashIfSandboxed (default true), except in plan mode. Same text-matching evasion caveats as deny rules.

evidence.quote: List the tool uses that prompt you for confirmation even in a permission mode that would otherwise approve them, such as `acceptEdits` or `bypassPermissions`.
Claude Code doesn't auto-approve the following in any mode, including `bypassPermissions`.
Content-scoped ask rules like `Bash(git push *)` still force a prompt

tool_rules.how: Same allow/ask/deny arrays with tool-specific specifiers: Read(path) (Read, Grep, Glob, LSP), Edit(path) (Edit, Write, NotebookEdit), WebFetch(domain:host), WebSearch (bare only), Agent(SubagentName), Skill(name), mcp__server__tool, PowerShell(...), Cd(path). Deny/ask rules can match any top-level scalar input parameter, e.g. Agent(model:opus) or Bash(run_in_background:true); deny/ask accept tool-name globs such as "*" or "mcp__*". --tools restricts the built-in tool set. Example: {"permissions": {"deny": ["WebSearch", "Agent(Explore)", "Edit(//etc/**)"], "allow": ["WebFetch(domain:docs.python.org)"]}}
tool_rules.limits: Path rules for Write, NotebookEdit, Glob or MultiEdit are accepted but never consulted (use Edit/Read). WebSearch has no domain specifier. WebFetch prompts by default except for a built-in set of preapproved documentation domains. A bare deny removes the tool from context; EndConversation cannot be denied while any other tool remains. Parameter rules cannot target a tool's primary field (command, file_path, url).

evidence.quote: All of these accept the same rule format, `ToolName(specifier)`. The specifier depends on the tool, and several tools share a format
WebSearch permission rules take no specifier. A bare `WebSearch` entry in `allow` or `deny` is the only form.
Deny and ask rules can match a top-level input parameter on any built-in tool with `Tool(param:value)`.
If you write a path rule for `Write`, `NotebookEdit`, `Glob`, or the legacy `MultiEdit` tool instead, Claude Code accepts the rule but never consults it

file_read_deny.how: permissions.deny Read rules (gitignore syntax; // = absolute, ~/ = home, / = relative to settings source). Example: {"permissions": {"deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Read(~/.ssh/**)"]}}. With sandbox.enabled true, Read deny rules are also added to the sandbox's denyRead list, so they become OS-level for shell commands too; sandbox-only keys: sandbox.filesystem.denyRead or sandbox.credentials.files [{"path": "~/.ssh", "mode": "deny"}] with sandbox.enabled true. permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories: true refuses file-tool reads outside working directories in every mode.
file_read_deny.limits: Shell reads are stopped at OS level only when the sandbox is on (sandbox.enabled, off by default, unavailable on native Windows). Without it, Read deny rules cover Read/Grep/Glob/LSP, @-mentions, IDE-shared context, Edit/Write on the same path, Bash file commands Claude Code recognizes (cat, head, tail, sed, tee) and `<` redirect targets, but NOT `grep -r pattern .` run from the directory or any script/subprocess that opens files itself. Even with the sandbox on, excludedCommands, approved unsandboxed retries (unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false), MCP servers and hooks are outside it. The sandbox's default read policy allows the whole machine, including ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials, so nothing is read-denied until you configure it.

evidence.quote: file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, such as `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, and `tee`
They don't apply to a command that reads files without naming them, such as `grep -r pattern .`
Claude Code adds your permission rules to the same lists: `Edit` allow and deny rules to `allowWrite` and `denyWrite`, `Read` deny rules to `denyRead`
Most of the machine, including credential files such as `~/.ssh` and `~/.aws/credentials`
Claude Code doesn't refuse shell commands the same way

file_write_scope.how: File tools: writes outside the working directory and additionalDirectories prompt in Manual/acceptEdits; Edit allow/deny rules (e.g. "deny": ["Edit(//etc/**)"]); protected paths (.git, .claude, .vscode, shell rc files, .mcp.json, etc.) never auto-approved outside bypassPermissions. Shell: with sandbox.enabled true, writes are OS-limited to cwd, a per-user temp dir and added directories; widen with sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite, narrow with denyWrite. --restricted confines file tools to the working directories.
file_write_scope.limits: Shell writes are confined at OS level only with the sandbox on (off by default; unavailable on native Windows; falls back to unsandboxed if it cannot start unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is true). Without it, an approved Bash command can write anywhere the user can. For file tools the working-directory boundary is a prompt, not a hard block, and it is skipped in bypassPermissions; hard path blocks need Edit deny rules or --restricted. Claude may retry a failed command unsandboxed (dangerouslyDisableSandbox) unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false, and excludedCommands run with full access.

evidence.quote: The boundary is a permission prompt, so a Bash command you approve can still write anywhere your user account can
The working directory, a per-user temp directory, and directories you've added.
Writes to a small set of paths are never auto-approved, except in `bypassPermissions` mode

network_control.how: Shell commands: sandbox.network.allowedDomains / deniedDomains (exact hosts, leading `*.` wildcards, IPs, optional :port) enforced by a local proxy; sandbox.network.strictAllowlist (user/managed/--settings) and managed-only sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly refuse unlisted hosts without prompting. WebFetch tool: WebFetch(domain:...) allow/ask/deny rules (also merged into the sandbox lists). WebSearch: whole-tool allow/deny only. Example: {"sandbox": {"enabled": true, "network": {"allowedDomains": ["github.com", "*.npmjs.org"]}}, "permissions": {"deny": ["WebSearch"]}}
scopes: project_shared (allowedDomains ignored when sandbox is admin-required or strictAllowlist is set)
network_control.limits: Requires the sandbox (off by default). The proxy decides on hostname and does not inspect TLS by default, so domain fronting is possible; tools that ignore proxy variables (ssh, DB drivers, UDP) simply cannot connect. Without the sandbox, network control for shell is only command-text deny rules such as Bash(curl *). allowedDomains does not restrict WebFetch, and MCP servers, hooks and excludedCommands are outside the sandbox. In bypassPermissions, hosts outside the allowlist are allowed unless strictAllowlist/allowManagedDomainsOnly is on. Hosts resolving to local/link-local addresses (e.g. 169.254.169.254) are refused by default.

evidence.quote: Connections go through a proxy on your machine that checks each host against your allowed domains, which start empty.
A `denyRead` entry doesn't stop the Read tool, and `allowedDomains` doesn't limit WebFetch
code running inside the sandbox can potentially use domain fronting or similar techniques to reach hosts outside the allowlist
WebFetch rules use a `domain:` prefix and match against the hostname of the requested URL.

sandbox.how: Built-in Bash sandbox on @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime: macOS Seatbelt; Linux and WSL2 bubblewrap + socat (optional seccomp filter for Unix sockets); native Windows not supported. Off by default. Keys: sandbox.enabled, failIfUnavailable, autoAllowBashIfSandboxed (default true), allowUnsandboxedCommands (default true), excludedCommands, filesystem.{allowWrite,denyWrite,denyRead,allowRead,disabled,allowManagedReadPathsOnly}, network.{allowedDomains,deniedDomains,strictAllowlist,allowManagedDomainsOnly,...}, credentials.{files,envVars} (deny or mask), enableWeakerNestedSandbox, enableWeakerNetworkIsolation, allowAppleEvents. Example managed enforcement: {"sandbox": {"enabled": true, "failIfUnavailable": true, "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false}}
sandbox.limits: Covers Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their children only; file tools, WebFetch/WebSearch, MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers, status line and apiKeyHelper run with full user access. `!` commands typed by the user run unsandboxed in most sessions. Silent fallback to unsandboxed if dependencies are missing unless failIfUnavailable. Project files cannot set filesystem.disabled, allowAppleEvents, strictAllowlist or credential masking, but can set excludedCommands, allowedDomains and the weaker-isolation flags unless the sandbox is admin-required (allowUnsandboxedCommands false via managed/--settings, or allowManagedDomainsOnly). Whole-process isolation options: sandbox-runtime wrapper, dev container, cloud sessions in Anthropic VMs.

evidence.quote: The sandbox is off by default.
The sandbox covers shell commands only. Claude's file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it.
By default, if the sandbox can't start because a dependency is missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code runs commands without sandboxing.
Project settings in `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json` can't, so a checked-out project can't switch filesystem isolation off.
A repository's `.claude/settings.json` can too, unless the sandbox is admin-required.

approval_modes.how: Modes (config value / UI label): default (Manual; alias manual), acceptEdits, plan, auto (classifier model reviews actions), dontAsk (anything that would prompt is denied), bypassPermissions. Set with permissions.defaultMode, --permission-mode <mode>, --dangerously-skip-permissions (= bypassPermissions), --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions (adds bypass to the Shift+Tab cycle), --permission-prompts none (-p: deny anything that would prompt), --permission-prompt-tool, --restricted. VS Code: claudeCode.initialPermissionMode and claudeCode.allowDangerouslySkipPermissions. Built-in default since v2.1.283: auto for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions; -p/SDK default is `default` (auto in sessions that do not fetch feature flags, v2.1.285+). Example: {"permissions": {"defaultMode": "acceptEdits"}}
approval_modes.project_can_set_most_permissive: No, since v2.1.257 (September 1, 2026): defaultMode "bypassPermissions" (and "auto") in .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json is ignored and the session starts in Manual. Before v2.1.257 a project file could set bypassPermissions. A project can still set acceptEdits, plan, dontAsk or default. skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt cannot be set by a repository. The VS Code extension never reads project files for the starting mode; cloud sessions ignore bypassPermissions/dontAsk from any settings file.
approval_modes.limits: bypassPermissions still honors deny rules, ask rules, critical-path rm prompts and requiresUserInteraction tools, but allow rules are irrelevant and protected-path writes are allowed. It refuses to start as root/sudo on Linux/macOS outside a recognized sandbox. First interactive use shows a one-time acceptance dialog that writes skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt to ~/.claude/settings.json. Auto mode is the default and relies on a classifier; the docs warn it does not guarantee safety.

evidence.quote: With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions.
If you set `"bypassPermissions"` in those two files, it doesn't take effect either, and the session starts in Manual mode.
Before v2.1.257, `bypassPermissions` took effect from any file.
Changed `defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"` in `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json` to be ignored, like `"auto"`
An untrusted repository can't skip the dialog for you.

bypass_lockout.how: permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable" (rejects --dangerously-skip-permissions, ignores agent frontmatter permissionMode: bypassPermissions, makes hook setMode bypass a no-op) and permissions.disableAutoMode (or top-level disableAutoMode): "disable". Put them in managed settings so lower scopes cannot remove them. Example: {"permissions": {"disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable", "disableAutoMode": "disable"}}. --restricted (or CLAUDE_CODE_RESTRICTED=1 in the launch environment) also refuses bypassPermissions. Desktop on Team/Enterprise: organization policy controls the bypass toggle.
bypass_lockout.limits: Client-side control. A local administrator can edit the managed file/profile; server-managed settings are not fetched for third-party providers (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry), a non-default ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, or a login to another organization, and only apply to clients new enough to fetch them; a modified binary bypasses everything. HKCU registry policy is user-writable. Before v2.1.223 an agent definition's bypassPermissions ignored the org disable policy.

evidence.quote: Prevent anyone from entering `bypassPermissions` mode. Claude Code then rejects the `--dangerously-skip-permissions` flag
Administrators can turn it off for the organization by setting `permissions.disableAutoMode` to `"disable"` in managed settings.
they operate as a client-side control, not a security boundary. On unmanaged devices, a user doesn't need admin or sudo access to bypass them.
a developer who is an administrator on the machine can edit the managed source itself

mcp_server_allowlist.how: allowedMcpServers / deniedMcpServers entries with exactly one of serverName, serverCommand (exact argv array) or serverUrl (wildcard pattern); managed-only allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true locks the allowlist to managed values; managed-mcp.json gives exclusive control (empty map disables MCP); managedMcpServers provides servers; strictPluginOnlyCustomization ["mcp"]; disableSideloadFlags rejects --mcp-config; disabledMcpjsonServers rejects .mcp.json servers; --strict-mcp-config. Example: {"allowManagedMcpServersOnly": true, "allowedMcpServers": [{"serverName": "github"}, {"serverUrl": "https://mcp.example.com/*"}], "deniedMcpServers": [{"serverCommand": ["npx", "-y", "evil-mcp"]}]}
mcp_server_allowlist.limits: Without allowManagedMcpServersOnly, allowedMcpServers merges from every scope (a soft allowlist that user or project files can widen). Denylist wins over allowlist and merges from all scopes. Built-in servers (Claude in Chrome, IDE server) are exempt from the allowlist and in-process sdk servers from both lists. Project .mcp.json servers require a per-server approval prompt interactively, but -p/SDK/cloud sessions load them without asking, and bypassPermissions sessions with skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt skip the prompt. managed-mcp.json cannot be delivered via server-managed settings.

evidence.quote: Claude Code blocks any server that doesn't match an entry wherever it's defined, including plugin servers
Entries from every file merge into one allowlist unless `allowManagedMcpServersOnly` is set.
When you deploy a `managed-mcp.json` file, Claude Code loads only these MCP servers
Claude Code also skips the prompt in a session you start in `bypassPermissions` mode with `skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt` set in your user settings or in managed settings.

mcp_tool_rules.how: Permission rules on MCP tool names: mcp__<server> or mcp__<server>__* (all tools of a server), mcp__<server>__<tool>, globs such as mcp__github__get_*; deny/ask may use "mcp__*". Example: {"permissions": {"allow": ["mcp__github__get_*"], "deny": ["mcp__github__delete_repo"]}}. Parameter-level rules for MCP tools only via --disallowedTools. Servers can mark tools _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"] to force a prompt every call.
mcp_tool_rules.limits: Allow globs must start with a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix; unanchored allow globs are skipped. Settings files skip any mcp__ rule with parentheses. Rules key on the configured server name, so a renamed server escapes name-based rules; hooks receive an mcp_server.source field for provenance. Org-level claude.ai connector tools set to ask override allow rules.

evidence.quote: `mcp__puppeteer__puppeteer_navigate` matches the `puppeteer_navigate` tool provided by the `puppeteer` server
Allow rules accept tool-name globs only after a literal `mcp__<server>__` prefix.
When Claude Code loads a settings file, it skips any `mcp__` rule that has parentheses.

hooks_blocking.how: hooks.PreToolUse (fires for every tool, including MCP tools, except EndConversation). Input on stdin (or HTTP POST body): session_id, prompt_id, transcript_path, cwd, permission_mode, hook_event_name, tool_name, tool_input, tool_use_id, plus mcp_server {name, source} for MCP tools. Block by exiting 2 (stderr becomes the reason) or by printing JSON {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": "..."}}; other decisions: ask, allow, defer (-p only), and updatedInput rewrites the call. Other blocking events: PermissionRequest (decision.behavior allow/deny), UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, ConfigChange (not for policy_settings), PostToolBatch, PreCompact, PreModelSwitch, Elicitation, Stop/SubagentStop/TaskCompleted. Handler types: command, http, mcp_tool, prompt, agent. Example: {"hooks": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "~/.claude/hooks/check-bash.sh", "onFailure": "block"}]}]}}
hooks_blocking.limits: Fail-open by default: exit codes other than 0/2, crashes, missing scripts and timeouts do not block unless onFailure: "block" is set (v2.1.295+). A hook "allow" cannot override deny/ask rules; deny precedence is deny > defer > ask > allow across hooks. @-file mentions in the prompt bypass PreToolUse. managed allowManagedHooksOnly limits hooks to managed, SDK and force-enabled plugin hooks; disableAllHooks outside managed settings cannot disable managed hooks, and a project's disableAllHooks: false overrides a user's true.

evidence.quote: To block the action instead, set `"onFailure": "block"` on a `command` or `http` hook.
`PreToolUse` | Yes | Blocks the tool call
In addition to the common input fields, PreToolUse hooks receive `tool_name`, `tool_input`, and `tool_use_id`.
PreToolUse hook decisions don't bypass permission rules.
A timed-out `command`, `http`, or `mcp_tool` hook doesn't block the tool call.
a `"disableAllHooks": false` in a project's `.claude/settings.json` overrides a `true` in your user settings.

managed_policy.how: Managed settings (same JSON shape as settings.json) via server-managed settings (claude.ai admin console or Claude apps gateway), MDM (macOS com.anthropic.claudecode profile, Windows HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode), or files: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json, /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json (+ managed-settings.d/*.json, managed-mcp.json). Managed-only keys include allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, allowManagedHooksOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly, managedMcpServers, sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly, sandbox.filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly, strictKnownMarketplaces, blockedMarketplaces, strictPluginOnlyCustomization, disableSideloadFlags, forceRemoteSettingsRefresh, disableCommandPluginSources, policyHelper, managedSourcesBehavior. Any key can be set in managed settings and then cannot be overridden. Example: {"permissions": {"deny": ["Read(./.env)"], "disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable"}, "allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly": true}
managed_policy.limits: Client-side enforcement (see bypass_lockout). Default first-wins means only one managed source applies. Some keys honor a stricter lower-level value. Invalid managed entries mostly fail closed (e.g. invalid allowedMcpServers enforced as empty), but requiredMinimumVersion/requiredMaximumVersion fail open. Server-managed changes to hooks/env need the developer to accept an approval dialog. A managed `model` is a default, not a lock.

evidence.quote: Claude Code applies them above every other level, so no user, project, local, or `--settings` value overrides them
Linux and WSL: `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`
Claude Code uses the highest-ranked source that delivers at least one policy key and ignores the rest rather than merging them

repo_config_trust.how: Interactive sessions show a workspace trust dialog the first time Claude Code starts in an untrusted folder (keyed on the git repository root; stored as projects["<path>"].hasTrustDialogAccepted in ~/.claude.json; never persisted when started in the home directory). The dialog lists the allow rules and additional directories the folder would grant. deny and ask rules apply immediately. permissions.allow, additionalDirectories, most env values, hooks/helper commands and extraKnownMarketplaces wait for trust. Project .mcp.json servers additionally need per-server approval, and a repo cannot self-approve them while untrusted. claude -p and Agent SDK sessions never show the dialog.
scopes: project_local (when git-tracked or .claude is a symlink)
repo_config_trust.can_repo_weaken_safety: Cannot (current versions): start in bypassPermissions or auto via defaultMode (ignored from project/local since v2.1.257 for bypass); set skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt; set sandbox.filesystem.disabled, allowAppleEvents, strictAllowlist, credential masking or autoMode rules; lift a user's blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories or allowUnsandboxedCommands: false (v2.1.285+); turn telemetry export on or redirect it. Can, once the folder is trusted: add broad allow rules (e.g. "Bash", effective in Manual/acceptEdits but dropped in auto mode); set defaultMode acceptEdits or dontAsk; register hooks, which run arbitrary commands and may return permissionDecision allow (deny/ask rules still apply); override a user's disableAllHooks: true with false; set enableAllProjectMcpServers to auto-approve its own .mcp.json servers; add sandbox excludedCommands, allowedDomains and weaker-isolation flags unless the sandbox is admin-required. how.hooks: post_run_command, post_mcp_tool_use and post_cascade_response_with_transcript are the documented way to build an audit trail.
how.admin_audit_log: No admin audit log of agent tool calls or permission decisions is documented.

limits: Analytics are aggregate counts, not per-decision records. The Devin CLI does not report analytics in hybrid deployments.

evidence.quote: per-tool call counts such as Code Edit, Run Command, Search Web, and MCP Tool
This script appends every hook invocation to a log file, creating an audit trail of all Cascade actions.
